opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really natural idea, and it's one we've thought about quite a bit. The intuition is appealing: if you want the model to learn about objects and how they move and interact, then mask out the objects and force it to predict them.

But I'm a bit cautious about it, for a few reasons.

First, it injects a lot of prior knowledge into what's supposed to be a self-supervised pipeline. An object detector was trained with labels, so it already encodes a particular human notion of what counts as an "object" and what's semantically meaningful. Part of what we're trying to understand with JEPA-style methods is how far you can get learning from the raw signal alone. If you lean on a detector, it becomes hard to tell how much of the representation quality comes from the self-supervised objective and how much is distilled from the supervised detector.

Second, it can bias the representation. A detector is good at the categories it was trained on, but the world is full of stuff that isn't a neat bounding box: fluids, deformable things, textures, background dynamics, parts of objects, the interactions between them. If you only mask what the detector thinks is important, you may get a model that's very good at those categories and blind to everything else.

Third, the masking strategy that works well in practice is already doing something similar implicitly. In V-JEPA we use fairly large spatiotemporal block masks, what we call multi-block masking, where a region is masked across the whole temporal extent of the clip. Because the blocks are big and persistent in time, the model can't solve the task by copying from neighboring frames or interpolating low-level texture. It has to reason about what's going on in that region at a higher level. So you get a lot of the "predict something semantic" pressure without telling the model what's semantic.

That said, I don't think it's a bad experiment. It's a useful diagnostic: if object-centric masking helped a lot, it would tell you the default masks are leaving signal on the table. And there are softer versions that seem promising, like adapting the masks from the model's own representations, or curriculum-style approaches, so the notion of what's meaningful comes from the model rather than an external labeled system.

So my view is: interesting as a probe, but for the core recipe I'd rather keep the masking generic and let the objective discover what matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the detector’s supervised prior and potential representation bias, but does not identify its computational cost as an obstacle to efficient learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's a really natural question, and it's one we actually thought about quite a bit. The short answer is that we deliberately avoided it, and the reason comes down to what we were trying to accomplish with V-JEPA in the first place.

The whole philosophy behind the JEPA family of models is self-supervised learning. We want the model to learn useful representations from raw video without any labels, without any human annotation in the loop. If you plug in an object detector to decide where to mask, you've kind of smuggled supervision back in through the side door. That detector was trained on labeled data, somebody drew those bounding boxes, somebody decided which categories count as objects. So now your "self-supervised" representation is downstream of all of those human decisions, and you've inherited the detector's biases about what matters in a scene. If the detector doesn't know about some object category, it's not going to be masked in a meaningful way, and that limits what the model can discover.

There's also a scalability argument. Part of the appeal of this approach is that you can just pour in more unlabeled video and the method keeps working. The moment you depend on a detector, you're bottlenecked on how good that detector is across all the domains you care about, and you'd need to run it over every frame of your pretraining data, which is expensive.

So what we did instead was quite simple. We mask large spatial blocks and we extend those masks across the entire temporal dimension of the clip. The intuition is that if you mask a big enough region, and you mask it consistently through time, then the model can't just copy information from a neighboring frame or interpolate from surrounding pixels. It actually has to reason about what's in that region and how it evolves. And a large contiguous block is very likely to cover a semantically meaningful chunk of the scene, an object or a big part of one, even without knowing where objects are. We found that this multi-block masking strategy with a high masking ratio was really key, and it works without any notion of objectness baked in.

Now, I don't want to say object-aware masking is a bad idea in general. There's interesting work exploring it, and you can imagine a curriculum where the model's own representations are used to propose regions, which keeps things self-supervised. That bootstrapping direction is one I find much more appealing than relying on an external detector. But for V-JEPA, the point was to show that you can get strong, semantic video representations with a very minimal, generic recipe, and the simple spatiotemporal block masking turned out to be enough.

r001.rationale: The response says a detector would need to run over every pretraining frame and that this would be expensive, identifying computational cost as an obstacle.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s an interesting direction. An object detector could help you select regions that correspond to meaningful objects, so you could ask the model to predict an entire object rather than a random portion of the video. But you’re also introducing the detector’s prior knowledge into the learning process—its definition of what an object is and which objects matter.

The motivation with V-JEPA is to see how much of that structure can emerge from learning to predict masked regions, without having to specify the semantic units beforehand. If the visible context makes a missing region too easy to predict, you may not need much understanding to solve the task. So the masking strategy matters, but it doesn’t necessarily have to be object-aware to create a useful learning problem. I’d view an object detector as an interesting comparison, rather than something the approach fundamentally needs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the detector’s prior knowledge and its role as a comparison, but does not identify computational cost as an obstacle to efficient learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a reasonable approach, but it introduces an assumption about what’s meaningful in the video. If you use an object detector to choose your masks, you’re relying on the detector’s categories and whatever supervision went into training it. We’d like those semantic concepts to emerge from the learning process itself.

With V-JEPA, we mask regions without needing to identify objects first and ask the model to predict representations of the missing content. To do that well, it has to learn relationships across space and time. An object detector could be useful, but the question is whether we can learn those representations without putting that knowledge into the masking procedure.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliance on the detector’s categories and training supervision, but does not identify computational cost as an obstacle.
